items.title: Acting Through Registers
items.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

items.title: Advances in endoscopic ultrasound for autoimmune pancreatitis: Tissue acquisition, imaging innovations, artificial intelligence, and multidisciplinary integrations
items.abstract: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is an immune-mediated inflammatory condition of the pancreas that can be difficult to differentiate from pancreatic malignancy and therefore remains challenging to diagnose. Type 1 AIP is the pancreatic manifestation of immunoglobulin G subclass 4-related disease and can be associated with other systemic fibro-inflammatory conditions. Type 2 AIP is characterised histologically by granulocytic epithelial lesions and is frequently associated with inflammatory bowel disease. Over the previous years, endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) has become an important part of the diagnostic work-up of patients presenting with suspected AIP, particularly when imaging studies demonstrate focal pancreatic enlargement, or a mass-like lesion. Recent advances in EUS imaging, including contrast-enhanced harmonic EUS and EUS elastography, may improve characterisation of the pancreatic lesion and help distinguish an inflammatory pancreatic process from a pancreatic malignancy. Moreover, EUS-guided tissue acquisition plays an important role in this context by allowing histological assessment of the lesion and hence helping exclude a malignancy. EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy is currently the preferred tissue acquisition technique, as it allows the preservation of tissue architecture, which helps facilitate the diagnosis of AIP. A multidisciplinary approach involving a panel of specialists in hepatopancreatobiliary endoscopy, hepatology, rheumatology, radiology, cardiology, nephrology, and histopathology is valuable for integrating the different components of the diagnostic work-up and guiding subsequent management. Finally, emerging artificial intelligence algorithms for EUS may support the diagnostic process and facilitate recognition of AIP. This review discusses current and emerging EUS techniques, tissue acquisition options, safety considerations, multidisciplinary integration and the potential role of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and management of AIP.

items.title: Advances on Anti-Cancer Combination Therapies Targeting DNA Repair Pathway, Epigenetics, Microbiomes and the Immune System
items.abstract: Modern pipelines integrating multi-omics data, chemical libraries, structural biology information and artificial intelligence are currently accelerating drug discovery and precision medicine. Aligned with these advances, the multi-omics profiling technologies enable the identification of unique genetic and epigenetic signatures for stratification of patients based on cancer specific target and vulnerability. Targeted therapies to specific receptor or enzyme mutated or overexpressed often fail because cancer cells can adapt quickly. Tumor cells overgrow driven by new gene mutation and parallel crosstalk of signaling pathways. Patients with cancer and the hereditary syndrome targets such as BRCA1/2, and emerging targets such as ATR, CHK1, WEE1, and POLθ, are hypersensitive to ionizing radiation and PARP inhibitors. Combining synthetic lethality inhibitors, chemotherapy and immunotherapy effectively kill cancer cells by breaking multiple survival signaling pathways. Antibodies to immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting molecules like PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 can improve survival of patients, though predictive immunotype remains challenging. Emerging pharmacological approaches combining either epigenetic modifiers, oncomicrobiotics or engineered bacteria sequentially convert tumors into a highly antigenic, T cell-inflamed, and checkpoint-responsive tumor, providing a mechanistically grounded framework for next-generation precision immunotherapy. However, large human clinical trials remain necessary to standardize protocols, biomarkers and long-term efficacy. Cancer vaccines have evolved through rational engineering synthetic mRNA encoding tumor-specific antigens or tumor-associated antigens. This will enable the next generation of truly therapeutic and preventive vaccines for many cancers. This review provides a timely synthesis of the basic mechanisms for rational multidrug treatments for cancers.

items.title: Advancing Environmental Sustainability: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Monitoring, Predicting, and Controlling Sulfur Dioxide Emissions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Air pollution from sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) emissions poses significant threats to environmental sustainability, public health, and climate change efforts. Despite advances in monitoring and regulatory frameworks, traditional methods often fall short in accuracy, scalability, and efficiency. This study explores the transformative potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in environmental monitoring, SO 2 emission prediction, and desulfurization. It utilizes a literature review of research from 2013 to 2025, assessing AI and ML models for air pollution monitoring, SO 2 emission forecasting, catalytic desulfurization, and SO 2 solubility in ionic liquids. Key findings reveal that AI‐driven models improve predictive accuracy and real‐time monitoring, optimizing desulfurization processes, enhancing air quality, and supporting environmental sustainability. The study highlights the importance of hybrid AI models, improved data collection, and energy‐efficient practices to overcome field limitations. It underscores AI's transformative role in mitigating air pollution, controlling SO 2 emissions, and supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Advancing Wheat Improvement through Multi-Omics and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plays a central role in global food and nutritional security, but its productivity is challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses. Its large, polyploid genome and extensive repetitive sequences complicate the identification of genetic variation and the dissection of complex agronomic traits. This review examines emerging genomic resources and the complementary contributions of transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and epigenomics to wheat improvement. High-throughput genotyping platforms, including SNP arrays, genotyping-by-sequencing and DArTseq, facilitate genetic diversity analysis and the identification of genomic regions associated with agronomic traits. Pan-genome approaches extend analyses beyond a single reference assembly by capturing structural, copy-number and presence–absence variation. Functional omics studies provide information on transcriptional regulation, protein responses, metabolite accumulation and chromatin-associated mechanisms involved in development and stress adaptation. The review also considers the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for integrating complex datasets, predicting yield-related traits, automating phenotypic assessment and supporting genomic selection. Examples from wheat demonstrate the potential value of combining molecular information with computational approaches, although the reliability of predictions depends on data quality, representation and appropriate validation. Together, these advances provide complementary tools for identifying candidate genes and interpreting genotype–phenotype relationships. Their integration with reliable phenotypic information and established breeding practices may support more efficient wheat improvement while acknowledging the technical and biological challenges of translating molecular findings into breeding outcomes.

items.title: Affective Bond Between AI-Generated Music and Human Listeners
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is being applied to create music in an ever-widening range, but it has not been determined whether the results can effectively convey human emotions. A controlled-variable experimental design is used to explore the causal relationship between information density in prompts and listeners' affective recognition of AI-generated music. Six AI-generated musical works were selected as the experimental stimuli under three increasing levels of prompt conditions: minimal emotional descriptions, prompts that added harmonic progression information, and detailed prompts including parameters such as instrumentation, vocal processing and dynamic changes. The results showed that listeners could not understand the creators' purposes in either the minimal-prompt or harmony-augmented situations. All 30 listeners were able to feel the emotion and structure that were desired, and they could do so after repeated instructions. The study also found that the audio outputs of AI music systems generally have logical discontinuities and perceptual incongruity without fine-grained human encoding intervention. This paper proposes that AI functions as a medium for music creation, and its affective communication performance is based on a closed-loop human intervention system at two stages: prompt engineering (information encoding) and generative evaluation (signal decoding). This study offers empirical support and practical paths for human-AI collaboration models in AI-assisted music creation.

items.title: AffectWorld: Benchmarking Emotion-Driven Future World Prediction
items.abstract: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested.We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion-Action-World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 233 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define eight metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of five SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos3) required world-state change scores of 0.100-0.280 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states.

items.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
items.abstract: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents' robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.

items.title: Agentic EEG Pipeline Synthesis Using Large Language Models and the Model Context Protocol
items.abstract: Electroencephalography analysis typically requires multistage processing pipelines for which configuration depends on recording characteristics and the intended analytical objective. Although automated pipelines improve reproducibility, they generally implement predefined processing sequences. We present an agentic framework in which a large language model (LLM) orchestrator synthesizes and executes task-specific EEG processing workflows by selecting, parameterizing, and ordering established signal processing components accessed through Model Context Protocol interfaces. Computational EEG processing and analysis operations are performed using established EEGLAB (version 2026.0.0) implementations running in MATLAB (R2026a) , while structured execution results and quality control information are returned to the orchestrator to support adaptation during execution. The framework is evaluated by examining tool-layer execution fidelity, independent pipeline synthesis, and the quality of the resulting EEG output relative to the established DISCOVER-EEG workflow. In an evaluation using eight resting state EEG recordings from four participants, mean epoch retention was 0.845 for the agent-generated pipeline and 0.843 for DISCOVER-EEG, while mean spectral entropy was 4.87 and 4.84 bits, respectively. Mean signal-to-noise ratio was 13.92 dB for the agent-generated pipeline and 11.14 dB for DISCOVER-EEG; however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously because the pipelines used different upper filter boundaries. A secondary analysis examined whether EEG processed using the generated pipeline retained features relevant to Alzheimer’s disease versus healthy control classification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of coupling LLM-based orchestration with EEG processing software to generate executable task-specific workflows with structured execution records and provenance. Further evaluation across larger datasets, independent synthesis runs, and additional EEG paradigms is required in order to establish repeatability and generalizability.

items.title: Agentic Embodied AI for Human–Robot Collaboration: Architectures, Technologies, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Human-robot collaboration has relied on task models that are specified in advance for each product. Embodied foundation models and agentic artificial intelligence change this premise, because a robot can now interpret an open goal, plan, act, monitor the outcome and recover from failure. This review examines what that change means for collaboration. A critical narrative review was conducted over 231 sources. Embodied intelligence, agentic intelligence, autonomy and collaboration are distinguished, and four collaboration modes are defined by the roles of the human and the robot. Four system architectures are compared: modular agentic, end-to-end embodied, hierarchical agentic embodied, and human-centred shared autonomy. Six groups of enabling technologies and five collaboration mechanisms, from autonomy allocation to failure recovery, are analysed. Applications in six domains, from manufacturing to domestic service, are assessed by the maturity of their evidence. Reported systems are validated mainly on single cells and short tasks, human factors are measured in few studies, and verified safety layers remain separate from learned reasoning. An evaluation framework and research directions for seven open challenges are proposed. The review gives researchers and system builders a basis for bringing embodied and agentic AI into human-robot collaboration and for evaluating the systems that result.

items.title: Agentic Robot Creation through Generation, Verification, and Revision
items.abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.

items.title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
items.abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

items.title: AI adoption and employees’ physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes in the information technology sector: The mediating roles of trust in ai and workload
items.abstract: BackgroundThe rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the information technology (IT) reshaping the work design, with significant consequences for employee well-being and ergonomics. While AI enhances efficiency through task automation, its influence on workload dynamics and ergonomic consequences remains not sufficiently understood, particularly in emerging economy contexts.ObjectiveGrounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework and informed by Sociotechnical Systems Theory, this study investigates the relationship between AI adoption and employees' physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes while examining the mediating roles of trust in AI and workload among information technology professionals in India.MethodsTo assess this, seven reflective constructs were measured. The AI adoption construct has three sun-dimensions: performance expectancy, effort expectancy and usage behavior/intention. Employee ergonomics has two sub-dimensions: physical ergonomics discomfort, cognitive ergonomics/digital fatigue, which are modeled as higher-order constructs. However, trust and workload dynamics are modeled as lower-order constructs. The higher-order constructs were assessed along with the lower-order constructs. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were carried out to unravel the structural relationships among the constructs, and hypothesis testing was performed using structural equation modeling.ResultsThe findings indicate that AI adoption significantly enhances trust in AI and reduces workload, Trust in AI is negatively associated with workload, while workload positively influences both physical ergonomic discomfort and cognitive fatigue. AI adoption also demonstrates a significant direct effect on employee ergonomics. The mediation analysis revealed that trust and workload fully mediated the relationship between AI adoption and ergonomics, whereas trust partially mediates the relationship between AI adoption and workload. The serial mediation results reveal partial mediation on role of trust and workload in the nexus among AI adoption and ergonomics.ConclusionConsistent with the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework, the findings demonstrate that AI functions simultaneously as a job resource and a source of new job demands. Trust in AI serves as an important psychological resource that reduces workload and enhances employees' physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes. Trust in AI emerges as a vital psychological mechanism that mitigates workload and enhances ergonomic outcomes. The outcome contributes to the development of human-centric AI implementation strategies by highlighting the importance of trust-building and workload management in designing sustainable, ergonomically sound workplaces.

items.title: AI and Digital Twins for Predicting Coastal Erosion and Infrastructure Vulnerability
items.abstract: Rising seas and extreme weather make reactive, 20th-century coastal management obsolete. This chapter argues that converging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies offer a necessary alternative: dynamic, virtual representations of coastal systems for anticipatory governance. It traces the shift from static models to coupled DT architectures integrating Earth Observation, IoT, BIM, and GIS. The text reviews operational machine learning applications, including sequence models for shoreline forecasting, convolutional segmentation, and physics-informed neural networks. Special attention is given to data-scarce regions, where transfer learning and generative modeling bridge instrumentation gaps. Finally, it examines how DT outputs inform capital budgeting and disaster preparedness. The chapter concludes that the true constraints on coastal DTs are not algorithmic, but rather data governance, institutional integration, and the communication of uncertainty.

items.title: AI Career Twin: A Human–AI Collaborative Framework for Dynamic Skill-Gap Analysis and Personalized Career Guidance
items.abstract: AI Career Twin is a proposed human–AI collaborative framework designed to support personalized career guidance, dynamic skill-gap analysis, and informed career decision-making. The framework addresses the limitations of traditional career recommendation systems, which often rely on static profiles and provide recommendations without considering evolving skills, changing industry requirements, or the uncertainty of available evidence. The proposed framework maintains a dynamic, time-indexed digital representation of an individual’s educational background, technical skills, professional experience, projects, certifications, career goals, and personal preferences. It integrates evidence-based skill assessment, labor-market analysis, explainable role recommendations, personalized learning pathways, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide transparent and context-aware career guidance. Key components of the proposed framework include: Dynamic skill profiling with separate proficiency and confidence estimates. Evidence-based skill-gap analysis using time-stamped labor-market information. Personalized career-role recommendations based on skills, goals, and constraints. Adaptive learning-path suggestions considering time, cost, and prerequisites. Retrieval-grounded AI mentoring with source citations and uncertainty handling. Human–AI collaboration through user feedback, corrections, and scenario-based career exploration. The paper presents the proposed system architecture, mathematical formulations, algorithmic methodology, and a structured evaluation protocol covering recommendation accuracy, skill-gap correctness, mentoring quality, and user interaction. Research Status: This publication presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation methodology. The system has not yet been implemented or experimentally evaluated. Future work includes prototype development, empirical validation, and user-centered evaluation. The research aims to establish a foundation for transparent, explainable, and evidence-based AI-assisted career guidance while preserving human control over career decisions. items.title: AI Code Synthesis, Autonomous Debugging, and the Evolution of the Software Engineering Lifecycle: Repository Graph Reasoning, SWE-bench Benchmarks, and Security Bounds
items.abstract: Abstract—The software engineering (SWE) lifecycle has transitioned from human-centric manual programming toward autonomous AI code synthesis and closed-loop program repair. Foundation models pre-trained on billions of source code tokens—including modern frontier models and specialized coding LLMs—have evolved beyond isolated function autocompletion toward whole-repository fault localization, cross-file patch synthesis, and dynamic regression test generation. However, deploying autonomous agentic coding frameworks in enterprise software development environments exposes acute structural vulnerabilities: contextual fragmentation across massive Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), patch-induced semantic regressions, dependency hallucination attacks (e.g., package typosquatting), and severe computational token overhead during multi-step debugging loops. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of autonomous AI code synthesis. We formalize program synthesis as directed exploration over Program Dependency Graphs (PDGs), establish the mathematical mechanics of execution-guided test-time search with verbal reinforcement feedback (Reflexion), and model repository-scale retrieval using tree-sitter AST parsing. Furthermore, we construct an empirical benchmarking testbed evaluating state-of-the-art coding architectures across 500 real-world open-source software engineering issues from SWE-bench Lite and SWE-bench Verified. Our findings demonstrate that while single-turn code generation models achieve only a 14.8% resolve rate, agentic tree-search architectures coupled with AST-guided repository graphs achieve a 46.2% issue resolution rate. Concurrently, execution-guided sandbox feedback reduces semantic patch regression by 64.8%, though AI-generated code introduces a 19.4% prevalence of unverified dependency inclusions. Finally, we formulate open research directions in neuro-symbolic program verification, verified formal specification synthesis, and automated zero-shot licensing provenance. Index Terms—AI Code Synthesis, Automated Program Repair (APR), SWE-bench, Program Dependency Graphs (PDG), Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), Repository-Level Reasoning, Software Security, Agentic Coding.

items.title: AI DEMOCRATIZATION OR AI CONCENTRATION? RETHINKING COMPETITIVENESS, TRADE INEQUALITY, AND GLOBAL MARKET INTEGRATION IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE.
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the global economy by reshaping productivity, innovation, international competitiveness, trade, global value chains, employment, and the distribution of economic power. While cloud-based applications, open-source technologies, and commercially available AI tools are broadening access to AI-enabled capabilities, the foundational resources required to develop, control, and capture value from frontier AI—including advanced computing capacity, specialised talent, research capabilities, investment, intellectual property, data, and digital infrastructure—remain substantially concentrated. Against this background, the study examines the emerging AI democratization–concentration paradox and evaluates its implications for global competitiveness, international trade, global value chains, international economic inequality, and global market integration. The study adopts a descriptive, analytical, and comparative research design based primarily on secondary data from internationally recognised sources, including the Stanford AI Index, UN Trade and Development, World Trade Organization, International Monetary Fund, World Bank, OECD, and other relevant international datasets and institutional reports. Evidence from the contemporary period, subject to data availability, is examined through descriptive statistics, trend analysis, cross-country comparison, and comparative interpretation, with particular attention to advanced, emerging, and developing economies. The analytical framework distinguishes three interrelated dimensions of AI participation: AI access, referring to the ability to use AI applications and services; AI capability, referring to the infrastructure, computing capacity, skills, data, research, investment, and innovation resources required to develop and effectively utilise AI; and AI control, referring to ownership or influence over foundational technologies, intellectual property, platforms, computing infrastructure, and other critical sources of AI-related economic value. The findings indicate that AI is becoming an increasingly important determinant of global competitiveness, with technological infrastructure, skilled human capital, research capacity, investment, and innovation ecosystems increasingly complementing conventional sources of competitive advantage. The study further finds that although AI access is expanding, genuine democratization remains uneven because the complementary capabilities required for productive and sustainable AI participation are unequally distributed. At the same time, frontier AI development, advanced computing, investment, specialised talent, intellectual property, and major technological platforms remain substantially concentrated, creating new forms of technological dependency and potential market power. AI is also found to have significant implications for international trade and global value chains by reducing transaction and coordination costs, improving productivity, facilitating digitally delivered services, and creating opportunities for technological upgrading, while simultaneously altering traditional sources of comparative advantage. The distribution of these benefits remains uneven, raising concerns regarding international economic inequality and technological divergence. The study further identifies a dual effect on global market integration: AI can deepen economic interdependence through trade, investment, digital services, and global value chains, while the concentration of critical AI capabilities can generate technological dependency and fragmentation. Overall, the study concludes that AI is neither purely democratizing nor purely concentrating; rather, it is producing a “diffusion of use with concentration of capability.” The future inclusiveness of the global AI economy will therefore depend not merely on expanding access to AI applications, but on strengthening infrastructure, computing capacity, skills, research, innovation, domestic technological capabilities, value creation, and greater control over the resources underlying AI

items.title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: An Overarching Review
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.

items.title: AI in the Clinical Exam Room
items.abstract: In the middle of an overnight emergency shift, a physician moves between patients while an ambient AI scribe quietly captures each conversation, a chart summarization tool distills a complex oncology history in seconds, and predictive models flag who might deteriorate, fall, or return within thirty days. This chapter steps into that exam room to examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping daily clinical work. It surveys the evidence behind ambient scribes, which large studies link to meaningful reductions in documentation burden and burnout, and behind machine learning tools that increasingly outperform traditional risk scores for sepsis, inpatient falls, and hospital readmission. It also tells the cautionary stories, the widely deployed sepsis model that missed most cases and flooded clinicians with alerts, and the celebrated cancer advisor that recommended unsafe treatments. The lesson that emerges is consistent: these systems deliver real value only when paired with clinical judgment, careful local validation, and physicians who remain firmly in the loop.

items.title: AI literacy for AI natives? A four-country comparison
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly mainstream in children's homes and everyday lives. Using neo-ecological theory as a conceptual framework and Yang et al.'s (2026) five-component AI literacy progression model as an analytical lens, this document analysis examined core ECEC curricula and related guiding documents currently in use in Australia, China, Japan, and South Korea to determine whether early childhood education and care (ECEC) guiding documents are keeping pace with the rapid development. The analysis reveals that the curricula of Japan and South Korea contain no explicit reference to AI literacy, prioritising human-to-human relationships and offline safety. China's national ECEC guidelines similarly contain no AI references. However, Shanghai's strategic action plan explicitly positions kindergartens within broader AI education initiatives, though without specifying pedagogical progressions for young learners. Australia demonstrates limited and uneven alignment across AI literacy components, with the strongest alignment in “Interacting with AI Agents” and no alignment in “Understanding Human-AI Relationships”. Young children’s development of AI literacy is thus likely to remain contingent on the home environment, where they may be interacting with AI agents and creating artefacts more than developing awareness of ethical considerations and risks. Wide differences in children's foundational AI literacy capabilities may entrench educational disadvantage along the lines of AI literacy as it becomes increasingly mainstream in society. We argue that curriculum-guiding documents should be strengthened by articulating explicit AI literacy learning priorities and developmental expectations for young children, accompanied by culturally responsive resources to equip educators to facilitate equitable learning.

items.title: AI Literacy for Leaders
items.abstract: This chapter builds AI literacy for leaders who have no technical background and no need to acquire one. The aim is judgment, not coding. It lays out a working map of the main technologies, from machine learning and deep learning through natural language processing, generative AI, computer vision, and robotics and explains each in language a board member could follow. It defines the few concepts that actually come up in the room: namely, training data, model architecture, and algorithmic bias. It offers a maturity model for gauging how ready an organization really is. And it closes by taking apart five stubborn myths about what AI can and cannot do.

items.title: AI Tutor, Online Course, or Both? A Randomized Experimental Pilot Study for Evaluation Capacity Building
items.abstract: Extension lacks literature comparing standalone generative artificial intelligence (AI) with structured professional development for capacity building. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study evaluated the effects of an asynchronous online course and a custom AI tutor on evaluation knowledge and self-efficacy among Cooperative Extension professionals. We conducted a randomized 2 × 2 factorial pilot study crossing access to an evaluation certificate course with access to a custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). Of 144 registrants, 78 provided matched pre- and post-test data, with attrition differing across conditions. Data were analyzed using a three-way mixed factorial ANOVA. Course access and GPT access each increased objective knowledge, with post-test means around 91% across treatment groups. No statistically significant additive effect was detected for knowledge gain. However, given a possible ceiling effect and limited statistical power, this result is inconclusive. Course access and GPT access each increased self-efficacy, but the combined condition produced the smallest self-efficacy gain among treatment groups. Because these estimates are based on participants who completed the study, findings are preliminary. If replicated, results suggest that Extension should combine AI tutors and coursework only when each modality provides known complementary value.

items.title: AI Utilization and User Satisfaction among Science Teachers and Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has significantly influenced contemporary educational practices, offering opportunities to enhance teaching and learning while raising concerns about effective and ethical integration. This study examines AI utilization and user satisfaction among science teachers and students, and analyzes its effects on satisfaction, usefulness, ease of use, and reliability. A quantitative research design involved 242 STEM students and 22 science teachers in the Division of Tacurong City. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling. Results showed high AI utilization among students (x̄ = 3.79) and very high utilization among teachers (x̄ = 4.21). Satisfaction was high among students (x̄ = 3.87) and very high among teachers (x̄ = 4.38). SEM findings for the combined sample (n = 264) revealed that AI utilization significantly influenced overall satisfaction (β = 0.465, R² = 0.217, p < .001), usefulness (β = 0.457, R² = 0.208, p < .001), ease of use (β = 0.336, R² = 0.113, p < .001), and reliability (β = 0.257, R² = 0.066, p < .001). Among students (n = 242), AI utilization also showed significant positive effects on satisfaction and all dimensions. Among teachers (n = 22), AI utilization did not significantly affect overall satisfaction, ease of use, and reliability, but strongly affected usefulness (β = 0.576, R² = 0.332, p = .005). The findings indicate that AI is widely utilized and positively perceived among science teachers and students.

items.title: AI VIRTUAL INFLUENCERS AND CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION: THE ROLE OF PERCEIVED AUTHENTICITY AND TRUST
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated virtual influencers are increasingly being used by brands to promote products and interact with consumers through social media platforms. Although virtual influencers provide advantages such as consistency, scalability, creative flexibility, and greater brand control, questions remain regarding whether consumers perceive them as authentic and trustworthy. The present study examines the influence of the perceived authenticity of AI virtual influencers on consumer purchase intention and investigates the mediating role of trust. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were assumed to be collected from 100 social media users familiar with virtual influencer content through a structured questionnaire. Perceived authenticity, trust, and purchase intention were measured using five-point Likert-scale items. Reliability analysis, descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, regression analysis, and mediation analysis were employed. The illustrative findings indicate that perceived authenticity has a significant positive influence on trust and purchase intention. Trust also demonstrates a strong positive influence on purchase intention and partially mediates the relationship between perceived authenticity and purchase intention. The study highlights that the effectiveness of AI virtual influencer marketing depends not merely on technological novelty or visual appeal but substantially on consumers’ perceptions of genuineness and trustworthiness. The findings provide implications for brands seeking to incorporate AI-generated personalities into influencer marketing strategies.

items.title: AI Washing and Stock Returns: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Firms
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital. Using AI-related keywords from annual reports, AI patents, and AI-related job postings of Chinese A-share firms from 2020 to 2025, we construct a firm-year measure to examine this disclosure-investment gap. We classify a firm as an AI washer when its AI-related disclosure is above the industry-year median, while both AI patent activity and AI-related recruitment remain below their corresponding medians. Firms meeting this definition are associated with lower annual stock returns, and the result remains qualitatively unchanged when we use alternative methods to identify AI patents. Additional tests point to two related market responses: AI washing is accompanied by more negative media coverage and weaker investor sentiment. The return discount is also more pronounced among firms with higher institutional ownership and among firms in regions with stronger local AI policy support. These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity. Instead, the impact of AI narratives on stock returns appears to depend partly on whether firms can support those narratives with technological development and hiring.

items.title: AI-Assisted Metadata Enhancement for Digital Image Collections: A Pilot Study of Vision-Enabled Language Models in Cultural Heritage Description
items.abstract: This study evaluates the efficacy of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) for remediating and creating metadata within the Pittsburgh City Photographer Collection. By comparing outputs from several OpenAI and Google Gemini models against a human-remediated baseline, the research identifies a significant performance gap between AI-assisted remediation and autonomous metadata creation. Findings demonstrate that while LLMs can help institutions “see” obvious visual features previously omitted from legacy records, they lack the specialized local knowledge required for authoritative description. Subject heading application failed to align with established taxonomies, and models frequently introduced inappropriate editorial “noise” in descriptions. Most concerning were the error rates: 20% of objects contained factual errors in titles or descriptions when baseline metadata was provided, jumping to 40% when no context was available. These errors represent a direct threat to archival integrity. The study concludes that the expertise required to detect these sophisticated hallucinations often exceeds the effort of original metadata creation. Consequently, the researchers determined that the risk of introducing errors outweighs the benefit of increased data volume. Rather than moving forward with AI for a 20,000-image backlog, the institution will focus on updating human-centered descriptive practices and documentation to ensure metadata accuracy and reliability.

items.title: AI-driven cognitive cyber defence for secure blockchain–cloud–IoT healthcare ecosystems
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of blockchain, cloud, and IoT has led to unprecedented challenges in terms of cyberthreats to this modern digital healthcare era, especially to Bioinformatics. Traditional security architectures such as Firewall Implementation, Static Encryption and Authentication methods often fail to address the challenges prevailing in the current era which demands dynamic surveillance. In order to combat these threats, there is a need for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Driven Cognitive Cyber Defence (AI-CCD) which works autonomously to address the adversarial threats across these interconnected ecosystems. AI-CCD leverages the application of Advanced Artificial Intelligence (AAI) algorithm for an intelligent, adaptive and autonomous threats detection and threat mitigation. AI-CCD highlights the role of autonomous threat hunting, Real-Time Response Systems (RTRS), and it proves the resilience of AI models against adversarial cyberattacks. The proposed AI-CCD framework embodies the principles of advanced algorithms such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Transformer-based models for Anomaly Detection, Threat Classification, and Situational Awareness via Explainable AI (XAI) which together support real-time decision-making in evolving threat landscapes.

items.title: AI-Driven Consumer Behaviour Analytics: Transforming Retail and Marketing Practices in Tamil Nadu, India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionising the realms of retailing and marketing through the use of analytics which help businesses understand consumer behaviour and predict purchase decisions as well as offer consumers a personalised experience. With the increasing prevalence of e-commerce, digital payment systems, apps and social media channels in use, vast amounts of consumer data have been generated. The possibilities offered by AI analytics are therefore many in emerging retail environments such as that in Tamil Nadu. The paper will investigate the use of consumer behaviour analytics driven by artificial intelligence as a means of revolutionising retail and marketing processes focusing on aspects such as personalisation, predictive analytics, recommendation systems, customer segmentation, sentiment analysis and AI-based customer engagement. The research will be based on consumer behaviour, marketing, analytics and digital transformation perspectives in order to illustrate how AI analytics could assist in purchase prediction, targeted communications, customer satisfaction, loyalty and decision-making in retail. According to the available literature, AI can be helpful in increasing the accuracy in marketing, engagement of customers, demand prediction, and operations efficiency; nevertheless, the role of AI in this respect depends on data quality, technological maturity, trust of consumers, and proper data handling practices. The issues of privacy, algorithmic bias, cost of implementation, digital maturity, and transparency continue to play an important role among limitations, especially for small retailers.

items.title: AI-Driven Object Detection for Projectile Localization on Trauma X-rays: An Analytical Study of Diagnostic Accuracy and Forensic Utility
items.abstract: Background: Trauma radiographs may reveal retained bullets or metallic fragments, and early localization can influence further imaging, surgical planning, safety assessment, and forensic documentation. Methods: This feasibility study used a fully synthetic, computer-generated tabular dataset of 400 case-level records divided into 240 training-design records, 60 validation-design records, and a 100-record held-out test set. The 400 records were not pixel-level radiographs: no DICOM, PNG, or other X-ray images were generated for model training, and no YOLOv9 neural network was trained. Instead, ground-truth labels, confidence scores, simulated detector outputs, a simulated time-constrained radiologist first pass, object-level matches, and processing times were produced by a fixed-seed probabilistic simulation (seed 9173) to demonstrate an evaluation framework. The test set comprised 70 projectile-positive and 30 projectile-negative records. Results: The simulated AI output yielded 65 true positives, 5 false negatives, 3 false positives, and 27 true negatives, corresponding to 92.0% accuracy, 92.9% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity, 95.6% precision, and a 94.2% F1 score; ROC-AUC was 0.972. The simulated radiologist first pass was correct in 83.0% of test records. In paired correctness analysis, AI alone was correct in 12 records and the radiologist alone in 3 (exact McNemar p=0.035). Of 145 synthetic annotated fragments, 136 were matched, with mean IoU 0.828, mAP@0.50=0.937, and mAP@0.50:0.95=0.593. Conclusion: These values are simulation outputs and do not constitute evidence that YOLOv9 detects projectiles on patient radiographs. The study demonstrates a reproducible analysis plan that requires validation on authentic multicentre radiographs, independent annotation, external testing, calibration, human-factors evaluation, and forensic governance before any clinical use.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN PERSONALIZATION AND AUTOMATED ASSESSMENT IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMSs) are widely used to organize learning materials, communication, assessment, and progress tracking. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) creates opportunities to make these systems more responsive to learners’ needs. This thesis examines two related applications: personalized learning support and automated assessment. It outlines how AI can use learning activity data to recommend suitable resources, identify topics that may require additional practice, and provide timely feedback. The paper also discusses limitations associated with data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and the need for teacher oversight. The study is conceptual and based on a review of relevant literature; it does not report original experimental measurements. It concludes that AI can support teaching and learning when it is implemented as an assistive tool within a transparent, privacy-aware, and educator-supervised LMS.

items.title: AI-enabled assessment: framework, perspective and educational outcomes
items.abstract: The development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT have raised concerns about assessment practice in higher education (HE). Prior studies have discussed the need to re-imagine and re-design assessment instruments; however, there is limited empirical evidence on how to effectively deploy this in practice. This paper proposes the TSD (task, scaffolding support and deliverable) framework to guide academics and education providers on how to effectively integrate AI and reflective practice into assessment design. By doing so, we adopt a mixed-method approach to investigate educational outcomes, tutors’ and students’ perspectives on the reflective AI-enabled assessment. This study collected data from UK University students (22 respondents) and tutors (24 participants) using a survey questionnaire and semi-structured interview questions, respectively. This study provides empirical support for positioning reflective practice as evidence of learning rather than being treated as a mere assessment activity. The findings show that AI output verification specific tasks need to be incorporated into AI-enabled assessment design. The results suggest that students perceived that our assessment strategy encouraged deeper learning, critical thinking and ethical awareness. Similarly, tutors were mostly positive with the adoption of the strategy, but some highlight the need for caution and multimodal approach .

items.title: AI-Enabled IoT Mobile Health Platform for Telemedicine and Predictive Diagnostics in Underserved Communities in Rural Nigeria
items.abstract: AI-enabled IoT mHealth could expand telemedicine and risk stratification in rural Nigeria, but implementation depends on infrastructure, awareness, trust, and clinical governance. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1,000 respondents from six rural communities assessed mobile access, telemedicine and IoT awareness, internet and electricity availability, willingness to use AI, trust, healthcare satisfaction, and perceived usefulness. Wilson 95% confidence intervals summarized binary outcomes. Results: Phone ownership was 74.1%, willingness 60.3%, and perceived usefulness 76.8%, whereas reliable internet was 20.0%, telemedicine awareness 26.9%, IoT awareness 17.9%, electricity availability 32.9%, and AI trust 50.0%. Poor or very poor healthcare access was reported by 59.5%. Conclusion: Social receptivity exceeds technical readiness. Deployment should prioritize offline-first telemedicine, clinician oversight, selective IoT integration, and local validation before predictive models are used clinically. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; mobile health; telemedicine; predictive diagnostics; edge computing; rural healthcare; Nigeria.

items.title: AI-Mediated Apprenticeship: Rethinking Follower Development in Servant Leadership Under GenAI Delegation
items.abstract: Generative AI can now perform routine and first-pass knowledge work that has also helped less-experienced employees develop. This creates a leadership problem for servant leadership, which treats follower growth as a constitutive priority. This article introduces developmental work access (DWA): the breadth and continuity of meaningful participation in development-bearing work across the part of a follower’s portfolio that a focal leader can materially allocate. It distinguishes general AI use from efficiency-first managerial AI delegation (EFAID). In EFAID, speed, cost, throughput, or reduced managerial burden guide delegation, while follower development is absent from the material allocation decision. Four propositions link servant leadership, EFAID, DWA, leader-designed AI-mediated apprenticeship (AMA), and role-relevant capability development. AMA comprises verified review, specification authorship, and reflective human–AI comparison. It is a design-side moderator; DWA records realised participation. This article also specifies how to measure eligible work, participation, breadth, continuity, portfolio compensation, and construct denominators. The model neither assumes that AI causes deskilling nor that AMA works in every setting. It identifies when manager-authorised delegation may restrict developmental participation and how leaders may reconstruct it while protecting genuine human execution.

items.title: AI-Simulated User Agents for Design Research: A Human–AI Collaborative Framework Leveraging Large Language Models
items.abstract: Traditional user research in design involves persistent tensions among scale, depth, and resource demands. We propose a three-tier conceptual framework for using large language models as simulated-user aids in design research. The evidence is separated by status: Studies 1 and 2 are company-confirmed aggregate commercial summaries and are reported descriptively, whereas Study 3 is an exploratory same-model prompt-format pilot. Study 3 compared a generic prompt with a framework-inspired structured prompt on 24 briefs using 14 included human-evaluator records from a mixed convenience sample and 140 evaluator–report ratings. The primary crossed mixed models found no condition coefficient at p < 0.05 and no Holm-adjusted advantage. Task-level Wilcoxon sensitivity results were likewise non-significant after Holm’s adjustment; forced choice was 5 structured versus 7 generic among 12 decisive responses (exact p = 0.774). The evidence therefore supports a bounded conceptual workflow and preliminary subjective report appraisal.

items.title: AI, Human Judgment, And Decision Reliability In High Tempo Military Operations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in modern military operations, influencing how commanders interpret sensor data, assess threats, and make rapid decisions under pressure. While AI improves situational awareness and accelerates operational tempo, it also introduces vulnerabilities such as fabricated outputs, misclassifications, and opaque decision processes. Human factors—including stress, uncertainty, and organisational pressure—further complicate decision reliability, especially in compressed timelines. This article uses a SWOT analysis to evaluate the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with AI‑enabled battlefield decision-making. It also examines how human judgment interacts with AI recommendations and identifies doctrinal and oversight mechanisms needed to preserve stability in modern conflict environments.

items.title: AIDCare: A Technical Proof-of-Concept for Integrating Personalized Nutrition, Physical Activity, and AI-Assisted Care in Diabetes Lifestyle Management
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Medical nutrition therapy and structured lifestyle self-management are fundamental to diabetes care, yet conventional mobile health tools typically track diet, physical activity, and glucose measurements in isolation, with limited connection to clinical oversight. This study presents AIDCare, an integrated mobile health platform that connects camera-based nutritional assessment, wearable physical activity tracking, physiological monitoring, and clinician-supervised conversational artificial intelligence (AI) to support personalized dietary and lifestyle self-management in diabetes. Methods: AIDCare links a patient mobile application with wearable sensors, backend analytical services, and an interactive clinician portal. Dietary assessment uses smartphone camera imaging to identify foods and estimate meal contents, specifically carbohydrates, protein, and dietary fiber, against nutritional reference data. Physical activity and energy expenditure are captured through smartphone and smartwatch motion sensors. To support contextual lifestyle guidance, an open-access medical conversational language model was adapted using 24,612 structured digital health and diabetes educational articles. A clinician-in-the-loop mechanism allows healthcare providers to inspect AI-generated recommendations and adjust personalization parameters. System feasibility was evaluated through benchtop and system-level testing without patient recruitment, using synthetic patient profiles across 400 data-acquisition pipeline trials and an intent-classification benchmark spanning nutrition, activity, glucose monitoring, and physician consultation. Results: Across the 400 software-pipeline trials, the platform achieved data acquisition, transmission, and processing completion rates of 97.5%, 96.5%, and 95.5%, respectively, with backend response times under 1.8 s. In the recommendation-intent benchmark, the medical language model achieved 81.0% accuracy, 83.5% precision, 79.0% recall, and an F1-score of 81.2%. The platform successfully linked image-based meal nutrient estimates (carbohydrate, protein, and dietary fiber) with physical activity metrics and physiological tracking within a unified interface under clinician supervision. Conclusions: AIDCare establishes the technical feasibility of a unified digital platform that integrates dietary nutrient estimation, physical activity tracking, and clinician-guided AI decision support for diabetes self-management. By bridging daily nutritional intake with metabolic tracking and professional oversight, the architecture provides a functional framework for personalized lifestyle care. Prospective clinical trials in patient cohorts are required to establish nutritional estimation accuracy against weighed food records, long-term user adherence, and clinical efficacy on glycemic control.

items.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence creates opportunities for students with visual impairments to access learning materials in adaptable formats, obtain descriptions of visual information, and receive support that responds to their pace of interaction. The availability of an application, however, does not constitute accessibility. This study analyses the dimensions of accessibility, the barriers that emerge, and the conditions required for meaningful participation in such learning. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed through thematic document analysis of 23 sources, comprising 19 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026 and four policy or accessibility-standard documents. The analysis yields a five-layer framework: operability; informational equivalence and modality flexibility; output reliability and verifiability; user competence and pedagogical mediation; and governance and infrastructure. Artificial intelligence can strengthen learning independence, yet it also generates new barriers: unlabeled controls, loss of meaning in visual materials, inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy risks, and unequal access to devices. The framework is offered as an initial audit reference requiring field validation.

items.title: Algorithms of Belonging: How AI-driven HRM Fosters Employee Resilience—A Self-concept Theory Perspective with Digital Competence as a Moderator
items.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence-driven human resource management (AIHRM) practices influence employee resilience and explores the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions underlying this relationship. Drawing on self-concept theory, the study examines perceived insider status (PIS) and organisation-based self-esteem (OBSE) as parallel mediators and digital competence as a moderator. Data were collected through a three-wave, time-lagged survey of 344 employees across India. Hypotheses were tested using moderated mediation analysis with bootstrapping and simple slope analysis. The results show that AIHRM is positively associated with PIS and OBSE, which enhance employee resilience. Both PIS and OBSE significantly mediate the AIHRM–resilience relationship. Digital competence strengthens the positive relationships between AIHRM and PIS and OBSE and enhances the corresponding indirect effects on resilience. The findings extend self-concept theory to AI-driven workplaces and identify digital competence as an important boundary condition. Practically, organisations should integrate AIHRM with digital competence development to strengthen employee self-concept and resilience.

items.title: All Talk and No Action?
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) has been proposed as a promising tool to enhance social competences in higher education, especially in resource-constrained counseling seminars. This study investigates the effects of a single-session VR-based training on university students’ counseling competence and self-efficacy. Forty-five students took part in a standardized counseling scenario delivered through a realistic social VR environment, interacting with a trained actor in real time. Pre- and post-training questionnaires assessed changes in self-efficacy and counseling competence, alongside measures of presence, realism, cognitive load, and perspective-taking. Results showed small, non-significant improvements in both outcome variables. Regression analyses revealed that perceived realism significantly predicted counseling competence, while presence and extraneous cognitive load influenced perspective-taking. However, the limited duration of the intervention and the absence of a control group constrain causal inferences. Despite these limitations, the study provides initial empirical support for the integration of VR technologies into counselor education and outlines key factors for effective implementation. Future research should explore adaptive, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced VR environments that allow for repeated practice and personalized feedback to fully realize the potential of VR in social skills training.
